big-o.title: Big-O and complexity
videos: Learn Big O notation in 6 minutes
big-o.focus: Big-O describes how running time or memory grows with input size n. Common classes in order: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n log n), O(n^2), O(2^n). Drop constants and lower-order terms. Space complexity counts the extra memory an algorithm uses.

arrays-hashing.title: Arrays and hashing
videos: Two Sum with a hash map (LeetCode 1)
arrays-hashing.focus: Hash maps and sets give average O(1) lookup, insert and delete. Typical uses: detect duplicates, count frequencies, find a complement (Two Sum), group items by a key (anagrams). The trade is extra O(n) memory for faster time.

exercises.q: Write two_sum(nums, target): return the indices [i, j] (i < j) of the two numbers that add up to target. Exactly one pair exists. Aim for one pass with a dict.
exercises.c:
def two_sum(nums, target):
    # Hint: store each number's index; for each x look up target - x
    return []

print(two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9))
exercises.test:
assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == [0, 1], 'basic case'
assert two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6) == [1, 2], 'pair is not at the start'
assert two_sum([3, 3], 6) == [0, 1], 'duplicate values'
assert two_sum([-1, -2, -3, -4, -5], -8) == [2, 4], 'negatives'

two-pointers.title: Two pointers
two-pointers.focus: Two indices move through a sequence, usually from both ends or at different speeds. Works on sorted or symmetric data: palindromes, pair sums, 3Sum. Typically O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

exercises.q: Write is_palindrome(s): True if s reads the same forwards and backwards, ignoring case and anything that is not a letter or digit. Use two pointers, not a reversed copy.
exercises.c:
def is_palindrome(s):
    # Hint: left and right indices; skip characters where not ch.isalnum()
    return False

print(is_palindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'))
exercises.test:
assert is_palindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama') is True, 'punctuation and case'
assert is_palindrome('race a car') is False, 'not a palindrome'
assert is_palindrome('') is True, 'empty string'
assert is_palindrome('.,') is True, 'only punctuation'
assert is_palindrome('0P') is False, 'digits count'

sliding-window.title: Sliding window
videos: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock (LeetCode 121)
sliding-window.focus: Keep a window [left, right] over a sequence and update the running state as it moves, instead of recomputing. Fixed-size windows (max sum of k items) and variable windows (longest substring satisfying a condition). Typically O(n).

exercises.q: Write max_window_sum(nums, k): the largest sum of any k consecutive numbers. Slide the window, adding the new item and removing the old one, instead of re-summing.
exercises.c:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    # Hint: sum the first k, then move one step at a time
    return 0

print(max_window_sum([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3))
exercises.test:
assert max_window_sum([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3) == 9, 'basic case'
assert max_window_sum([1, 2, 3], 3) == 6, 'window is the whole list'
assert max_window_sum([-5, -2, -9, -1], 2) == -7, 'all negative'
assert max_window_sum([4], 1) == 4, 'single item'

stack.title: Stack
stack.focus: A stack is last-in, first-out. Use it for matching brackets, undo-style state, and monotonic stacks (next greater element, daily temperatures). In Python a list gives O(1) append and pop.

exercises.q: Write is_valid(s): s contains only ()[]{} characters. Return True if every bracket is closed by the same type in the correct order.
exercises.c:
def is_valid(s):
    # Hint: push openers; on a closer, the top of the stack must match
    return False

print(is_valid('([]{})'))
exercises.test:
assert is_valid('()[]{}') is True, 'simple pairs'
assert is_valid('([{}])') is True, 'nested'
assert is_valid('(]') is False, 'wrong type'
assert is_valid('((') is False, 'unclosed'
assert is_valid(']') is False, 'closer with empty stack'
assert is_valid('') is True, 'empty string'

binary-search.title: Binary search
binary-search.focus: Halve a sorted or monotonic search space each step: O(log n). Watch the boundaries (left <= right, computing mid) and apply it to answers as well as indices, for example searching the eating speed in Koko Eating Bananas.

exercises.q: Write search(nums, target): nums is sorted ascending. Return the index of target, or -1. It must run in O(log n): halve the range each step.
exercises.c:
def search(nums, target):
    # Hint: left = 0, right = len(nums) - 1; compare nums[mid] with target
    return -1

print(search([-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], 9))
exercises.test:
assert search([-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], 9) == 4, 'found'
assert search([-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12], 2) == -1, 'missing'
assert search([5], 5) == 0, 'single item found'
assert search([5], 3) == -1, 'single item missing'
assert search([], 1) == -1, 'empty list'
assert search([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 1) == 0, 'first item'
assert search([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7], 7) == 6, 'last item'

linked-list.title: Linked list
videos: Reverse Linked List, iterative and recursive (LeetCode 206)
Linked List Cycle, Floyd's tortoise and hare (LeetCode 141)
linked-list.focus: Nodes linked by next pointers with no random access. Core moves: reverse in place, fast and slow pointers (Floyd cycle detection, middle node), a dummy head node to simplify edge cases, merging two sorted lists.

exercises.q: ListNode is given. Write reverse_list(head): reverse the list in place and return the new head. Walk the list once, re-pointing each node's next.
exercises.test:
def build(vals):
    head = None
    for v in reversed(vals):
        head = ListNode(v, head)
    return head

def to_list(node):
    out = []
    while node:
        out.append(node.val)
        node = node.next
    return out

assert to_list(reverse_list(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))) == [5, 4, 3, 2, 1], 'five nodes'
assert to_list(reverse_list(build([1, 2]))) == [2, 1], 'two nodes'
assert to_list(reverse_list(build([7]))) == [7], 'one node'
assert reverse_list(None) is None, 'empty list'

trees.title: Trees
videos: Binary Tree Level Order Traversal, BFS (LeetCode 102)
trees.focus: A binary tree node has left and right children. DFS (recursive pre-, in-, post-order) and BFS (queue, level order). Depth and height, inverting, and the BST property for ordered search. Recursion depth equals tree height.

exercises.q: TreeNode is given. Write max_depth(root): the number of nodes on the longest path from the root down to a leaf. An empty tree has depth 0. Recursion works well here.
exercises.test:
t = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(9), TreeNode(20, TreeNode(15), TreeNode(7)))
assert max_depth(t) == 3, 'balanced example'
assert max_depth(None) == 0, 'empty tree'
assert max_depth(TreeNode(1)) == 1, 'single node'
chain = TreeNode(1, None, TreeNode(2, None, TreeNode(3, None, TreeNode(4))))
assert max_depth(chain) == 4, 'skewed tree'

tries.title: Tries
tries.focus: A trie (prefix tree) maps characters to child nodes with an end-of-word flag. Insert, search and starts-with take O(L) for word length L. Good for autocomplete and prefix queries.

exercises.q: Implement a Trie class with insert(word), search(word) (exact word present) and starts_with(prefix). Store one dict of children per node plus an end-of-word flag.
exercises.test:
t = Trie()
t.insert('apple')
assert t.search('apple') is True, 'inserted word'
assert t.search('app') is False, 'prefix is not a word'
assert t.starts_with('app') is True, 'prefix exists'
assert t.starts_with('apx') is False, 'prefix missing'
t.insert('app')
assert t.search('app') is True, 'now a word'
assert t.search('') is False, 'empty is not inserted'
assert t.starts_with('') is True, 'empty prefix matches'

heap.title: Heap and priority queue
videos: Kth Largest Element in a Stream (LeetCode 703)
heap.focus: A priority queue backed by a binary heap. Python's heapq is a min-heap: push and pop are O(log n), peek is O(1). Use it for top-K, kth largest in a stream, merging sorted streams and scheduling. For a max-heap push negated values.

exercises.q: Write k_largest(nums, k): return the k largest numbers, biggest first. Use heapq (hint: heapq.nlargest, or keep a min-heap of size k).
exercises.c:
import heapq

def k_largest(nums, k):
    # Hint: a min-heap of size k keeps the k largest seen so far
    return []

print(k_largest([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2))
exercises.test:
assert k_largest([3, 2, 1, 5, 6, 4], 2) == [6, 5], 'basic case'
assert k_largest([3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], 4) == [6, 5, 5, 4], 'duplicates'
assert k_largest([1], 1) == [1], 'single item'
assert k_largest([5, 1], 2) == [5, 1], 'k equals length'

backtracking.title: Backtracking
backtracking.focus: Build candidates step by step, recurse, then undo the last choice (choose, explore, unchoose). Prune invalid branches early. Typical problems: subsets, permutations, combination sum, N-Queens. Worst case is exponential time.

exercises.q: Write subsets(nums): return every subset of the list (including the empty one) as a list of lists, in any order. Use choose, explore, un-choose.
exercises.c:
def subsets(nums):
    # Hint: recurse over the index; either include nums[i] or skip it
    return []

print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))

graphs.title: Graphs
graphs.focus: Nodes and edges, usually stored as adjacency lists. BFS (queue) finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; DFS handles connectivity, islands, cycle detection and topological order. Track visited nodes. Time O(V + E).

exercises.q: Write num_islands(grid): grid is a list of strings of '1' (land) and '0' (water). Count groups of land connected up, down, left or right. Use DFS or BFS and mark visited cells.
exercises.c:
def num_islands(grid):
    # Hint: for each unvisited '1', explore its whole island, then count +1
    return 0

print(num_islands(['11000', '11000', '00100', '00011']))
exercises.test:
assert num_islands(['11000', '11000', '00100', '00011']) == 3, 'three islands'
assert num_islands(['111', '010', '111']) == 1, 'one connected island'
assert num_islands(['000']) == 0, 'all water'
assert num_islands([]) == 0, 'empty grid'
assert num_islands(['101', '010', '101']) == 5, 'diagonals do not connect'

dp-1d.title: 1-D dynamic programming
dp-1d.focus: Dynamic programming stores answers to overlapping subproblems. In 1-D, dp[i] depends on earlier states: climbing stairs, house robber, coin change. Define the state, the recurrence and the base cases; use top-down memoisation or a bottom-up table.

exercises.q: Write climb_stairs(n): you can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. How many distinct ways are there to reach step n? Notice the pattern: ways(n) = ways(n-1) + ways(n-2).
exercises.c:
def climb_stairs(n):
    # Hint: keep only the last two answers
    return 0

print([climb_stairs(i) for i in range(1, 6)])
exercises.test:
assert climb_stairs(1) == 1, 'n = 1'
assert climb_stairs(2) == 2, 'n = 2'
assert climb_stairs(3) == 3, 'n = 3'
assert climb_stairs(5) == 8, 'n = 5'
assert climb_stairs(30) == 1346269, 'must be efficient for n = 30'

dp-2d.title: 2-D dynamic programming
dp-2d.focus: Two-dimensional state, such as dp[i][j] over two sequences or a grid: longest common subsequence, edit distance, unique paths. Fill the table from the base cases; time O(m*n), and space can often shrink to one row.

exercises.q: Write lcs_length(a, b): the length of the longest subsequence (characters in order, not necessarily adjacent) shared by strings a and b. Use a table dp[i][j].
exercises.c:
def lcs_length(a, b):
    # Hint: dp[i][j] = answer for a[:i] and b[:j]; match -> 1 + dp[i-1][j-1], else max of the two neighbours
    return 0

print(lcs_length('abcde', 'ace'))
exercises.test:
assert lcs_length('abcde', 'ace') == 3, 'ace'
assert lcs_length('abc', 'abc') == 3, 'identical'
assert lcs_length('abc', 'def') == 0, 'nothing in common'
assert lcs_length('', 'abc') == 0, 'empty string'
assert lcs_length('bl', 'yby') == 1, 'order matters'

greedy.title: Greedy
greedy.focus: Take the locally best choice at each step when it provably leads to a global optimum. Examples: maximum subarray (Kadane), jump game, interval scheduling. Justify it (for example with an exchange argument) or fall back to dynamic programming.

exercises.q: Write can_jump(nums): you start at index 0 and nums[i] is the maximum jump length from index i. Return True if you can reach the last index. Track the furthest index you can reach.
exercises.c:
def can_jump(nums):
    # Hint: furthest = 0; if i > furthest you are stuck
    return False

print(can_jump([2, 3, 1, 1, 4]))
exercises.test:
assert can_jump([2, 3, 1, 1, 4]) is True, 'reachable'
assert can_jump([3, 2, 1, 0, 4]) is False, 'stuck on the zero'
assert can_jump([0]) is True, 'already at the end'
assert can_jump([0, 1]) is False, 'cannot move at all'
assert can_jump([2, 0, 0]) is True, 'exactly enough'

intervals.title: Intervals
intervals.focus: Sort by start, then sweep, merging or inserting while tracking the current end. Typical problems: merge intervals, insert interval, meeting rooms. Sorting dominates, so O(n log n).

exercises.q: Write merge(intervals): a list of [start, end] pairs in any order. Merge all overlapping intervals (touching ends like [1,4] and [4,5] count as overlapping) and return them sorted by start.
exercises.c:
def merge(intervals):
    # Hint: sort by start, then compare each interval's start with the last merged end
    return []

print(merge([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]))
exercises.test:
assert merge([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]) == [[1, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]], 'basic case'
assert merge([[1, 4], [4, 5]]) == [[1, 5]], 'touching ends merge'
assert merge([[5, 6], [1, 2]]) == [[1, 2], [5, 6]], 'unsorted input'
assert merge([[1, 10], [2, 3]]) == [[1, 10]], 'one inside another'
assert merge([]) == [], 'empty list'
